claim: SWR1 is a conserved yeast chromatin remodeler that performs histone exchange on +1 nucleosomes adjacent to a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) at gene promoters.
source: SWR1, a conserved yeast chromatin remodeler that performs histone exchange on +1 nucleosomes adjacent to a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) at gene promoters.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of SWR1's function, drawing on established knowledge about this chromatin remodeler.

claim: SWR1 has a kinetic binding preference for DNA of NDR length as opposed to gene-body linker length DNA.
source: We demonstrate that SWR1 has a kinetic binding preference for DNA of NDR length as opposed to gene-body linker length DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F-G showing binding kinetics to different DNA lengths.

claim: ATP promotes SWR1 diffusion through nucleotide binding rather than ATP hydrolysis.
source: We found that various factors impact SWR1 scanning, including ATP which promotes diffusion through nucleotide binding rather than ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing that ATPγS (non-hydrolyzable analog) produces similar diffusion enhancement as ATP.

claim: The median diffusion coefficient of ATP-bound SWR1 is 0.024 μm2/s.
source: The median diffusion coefficient, 0.024 μm2/s, in the regime of helical sliding, would mediate rapid encounter of NDR-flanking nucleosomes at length scales found in cellular chromatin.
evidence: This value is directly measured from single-particle tracking experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: ATP-bound SWR1 slides until it encounters a protein roadblock.
source: ATP-bound SWR1 slides until it encounters a protein roadblock, of which we tested dCas9 and nucleosomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6 showing SWR1 diffusion is blocked by dCas9 and nucleosomes.

claim: A DNA-binding subunit, Swc2, plays an important role in the overall diffusive behavior of the SWR1 complex.
source: A DNA-binding subunit, Swc2, plays an important role in the overall diffusive behavior of the complex, as the subunit in isolation retains similar, although faster, scanning properties as the whole remodeler.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing that Swc2 DBD alone can diffuse on DNA with similar properties to full SWR1.

claim: A nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) of about 140 bp in length is flanked by two well-positioned nucleosomes at gene promoters in eukaryotes.
source: A particularly well-defined area of chromatin architecture is found at gene promoters in eukaryotes: a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) of about 140 bp in length is flanked by two well-positioned nucleosomes, one of which, the +1 nucleosome, sits on the transcription start site (TSS) (Bernstein et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2009; Yuan et al., 2005) and the nucleosome on the opposite side of the NDR, upstream of the TSS, is known as the −1 nucleosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature establishing this chromatin architecture.

claim: The +1 nucleosome is enriched for the noncanonical histone variant H2A.Z.
source: The +1 nucleosome is enriched for the noncanonical histone variant H2A.Z (Albert et al., 2007; Raisner et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies that established this enrichment pattern.

claim: In yeast, H2A.Z is deposited into the +1 nucleosome by SWR1.
source: in yeast, H2A.Z is deposited into the +1 nucleosome by SWR1 (Swi2/Snf2-related ATPase complex), a chromatin remodeler in the INO80 family of remodelers (Korber and Hörz, 2004; Krogan et al., 2004; Mizuguchi et al., 2004; Ranjan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies establishing SWR1's role in H2A.Z deposition.

claim: The insertion of H2A.Z into the +1 nucleosome is highly conserved and plays an important role in regulating transcription.
source: The insertion of H2A.Z into the +1 nucleosome is highly conserved and plays an important role in regulating transcription (Giaimo et al., 2019; Rudnizky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on the conservation and function of H2A.Z.

claim: The affinity of SWR1 for nucleosomes is enhanced by long-linker DNA.
source: The affinity of SWR1 for nucleosomes is enhanced by both long-linker DNA (Ranjan et al., 2013; Yen et al., 2013) and histone acetylation (Zhang et al., 2005), and both factors play a role in the recruitment of SWR1 to promoters.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating enhanced affinity with long-linker DNA.

claim: The affinity of SWR1 for nucleosomes is enhanced by histone acetylation.
source: The affinity of SWR1 for nucleosomes is enhanced by both long-linker DNA (Ranjan et al., 2013; Yen et al., 2013) and histone acetylation (Zhang et al., 2005), and both factors play a role in the recruitment of SWR1 to promoters.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study showing enhanced affinity with histone acetylation.

claim: H2A.Z is predominantly deposited on the long-linker distal face of the nucleosome.
source: A recent single-molecule study further showed that SWR1 likely exploits preferential interactions with long-linker length DNA by demonstrating that H2A.Z is predominantly deposited on the long-linker distal face of the nucleosome (Poyton et al., 2022), similar to what is observed in vivo (Rhee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to both a recent single-molecule study and an in vivo study.

claim: Facilitated diffusion has been shown to be essential for expediting the rate at which transcription factors and other DNA-binding proteins can bind their target compared to a 3D search alone.
source: Facilitated diffusion has been shown to be essential for expediting the rate at which transcription factors and other DNA-binding proteins can bind their target compared to a 3D search alone (Berg et al., 1981; Elf et al., 2007; Hannon et al., 1986; Ricchetti et al., 1988; von Hippel and Berg, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to foundational studies on facilitated diffusion.

claim: In vivo single-particle tracking found that chromatin remodelers have bound-state diffusion coefficients that are larger than that of bound H2B.
source: Recently published in vivo single-particle tracking found that chromatin remodelers have bound-state diffusion coefficients that are larger than that of bound H2B, hinting at the possibility that they may scan chromatin, but those studies could not distinguish between remodeler scanning and locally enhanced chromatin mobility (Kim et al., 2021; Ranjan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent in vivo single-particle tracking studies.

claim: It is not known if SWR1 or any other chromatin remodeler can linearly diffuse on DNA.
source: It is not known if SWR1 or any other chromatin remodeler can linearly diffuse on DNA, and therefore make use of facilitated diffusion to expedite its target search process.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: SWR1's core ATPase is a superfamily 2 (SF2) double-stranded DNA translocase.
source: Additionally, SWR1's core ATPase, like other chromatin remodelers, is a superfamily 2 (SF2) double-stranded DNA translocase (Nodelman and Bowman, 2021; Yan and Chen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on chromatin remodeler ATPase domains.

claim: The on-rate for SWR1 binding to 20 bp DNA was 1 × 10^6 M^-1 s^-1.
source: The on-rate for SWR1 binding to 20 bp DNA, the approximate size of linker DNA between intragenic nucleosomes in yeast, was 1 × 106 M−1 s−1.
evidence: This value is directly measured from the single-molecule colocalization experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Increasing the DNA length to 150 bp significantly increased the binding rate 36-fold to 3.6 × 10^7 M^-1 s^-1.
source: Increasing the DNA length to 150 bp, the approximate size of the NDR in yeast, significantly increased the binding rate 36-fold to 3.6 × 107 M−1 s−1.
evidence: This is directly measured from experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: kbind increased linearly with DNA length between 20 bp and 150 bp.
source: kbind increased linearly with DNA length between these two values (Figure 1F), indicating that as the effective concentration of DNA bp is increased, binding is also increased
evidence: This is demonstrated by the linear fit to the data in Figure 1F with R2 = 0.99.

claim: Longer DNA molecules could accommodate multiple bound SWR1 molecules.
source: This result suggests that longer DNA substrates may harbor more potential SWR1-binding sites. In support of this, we found that longer DNA molecules could accommodate multiple bound SWR1 molecules, with the likelihood of multiple binding events increasing with DNA length (see Figure 1E for an example trace).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: tbound for 20 bp DNA was 1.5 ± 0.3 s.
source: Whereas tbound for 20 bp DNA was 1.5 ± 0.3 s, tbound for SWR1 binding to 40 and 60 bp DNA increased to 9 ± 1.4 and 12 ± 5.8 s, respectively, which is the same within error (Figure 1G).
evidence: This value is directly measured from experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Once the DNA was 80 bp or longer, the lifetime increased dramatically to at least 30 s, the photobleaching limit of the measurement.
source: Once the DNA was 80 bp or longer, however, the lifetime increased dramatically to at least 30 s, the photobleaching limit of our measurement (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is measured from experiments shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Measurements at lower laser power showed that SWR1 remained bound to 150 bp DNA with a life time of approximately 3 min.
source: Measurements at lower laser power showed that SWR1 remained bound to 150 bp DNA with a life time of approximately 3 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is measured from experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: tbound was unchanged in the presence of ATP.
source: tbound was unchanged in the presence of ATP but was sensitive to ionic strength, decreasing with added salt (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: tbound was sensitive to ionic strength, decreasing with added salt.
source: tbound was unchanged in the presence of ATP but was sensitive to ionic strength, decreasing with added salt (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: tbound decreased in the presence of competitor DNA.
source: Curiously, tbound also decreased in the presence of competitor DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: As DNA length is increased, SWR1 tbound showed an approximately 120-fold increase.
source: In our in vitro experimental setup, as DNA length is increased, SWR1 tbound showed an approximately 120-fold increase.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A study utilizing single-particle tracking in vivo showed that the stable chromatin-bound dwell-time for a number of ATP-dependent remodelers is on the order of several seconds.
source: Indeed, a study utilizing single-particle tracking in vivo showed that the stable chromatin-bound dwell-time for a number of ATP-dependent remodelers is on the order of several seconds (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior in vivo study.

claim: The affinity of SWR1 for DNA greater than 60 bp is primarily limited by the on-rate.
source: The kinetic measurements presented here show that the affinity of SWR1 for DNA greater than 60 bp is primarily limited by the on-rate, suggesting the increased occupancy of SWR1 at longer NDRs observed in yeast (Ranjan et al., 2013) is a result of the increased probability of SWR1 finding the NDR, as opposed to an increase in the residence time of SWR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data in Figure 1F-G showing that on-rate increases more dramatically than off-rate with DNA length.

claim: Cy3-SWR1 bound to lambda DNA is mobile.
source: Cy3-SWR1 bound to lambda DNA is mobile, demonstrating that Cy3-SWR1 can move on DNA once bound and the movement did not appear to be unidirectional.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kymographs and tracking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The initial portion of the MSD versus time curve for SWR1 is linear, suggesting that diffusion is Brownian.
source: Therefore, we plotted mean square displacement (MSD) versus time and found that the initial portion of the curve is linear, suggesting that diffusion is Brownian (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MSD analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The diffusion coefficient observed (D1,obs) for Cy3-SWR1 was 0.013 ± 0.002 μm2/s in buffer alone.
source: The diffusion coefficient observed (D1,obs) for Cy3-SWR1 was 0.013 ± 0.002 μm2/s in buffer alone (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This value is directly measured from single-particle tracking experiments shown in Figure 2E, F.

claim: D1,obs for specifically bound Cy5-dCas9 is 0.0003 ± 0.0004 μm2/s, which is 40-fold smaller than Cy3-SWR1.
source: In contrast D1,obs for specifically bound Cy5-dCas9, an immobile reference with D1,obs of 0.0003 ± 0.0004 μm2/s, is 40-fold smaller than Cy3-SWR1.
evidence: This value is directly measured from experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SWR1 undergoes Brownian diffusion on nucleosome-free DNA.
source: These measurements clearly show that SWR1 undergoes Brownian diffusion on nucleosome-free DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MSD analysis and diffusion coefficient measurements in Figure 2.

claim: The MSDs of Cy3-SWR1 in the presence of ATP remained linear, showing that SWR1 does not translocate directionally on DNA.
source: The MSDs of Cy3-SWR1 in the presence of ATP remained linear, showing that SWR1 does not translocate directionally on DNA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MSD analysis in Figure 3A showing linear behavior.

claim: ATP increases the diffusion of SWR1 on DNA.
source: The increased slope of the MSDs in the ATP condition, however, does indicate that ATP increases the diffusion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing MSD slopes in Figure 3A with and without ATP.

claim: SWR1 diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ATP (D1,obs = 0.024 μm2/s ± 0.001) was not significantly different than diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ATPγS (D1,obs = 0.026 μm2/s ± 0.002).
source: SWR1 diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ATP (D1,obs = 0.024 μm2/s ± 0.001) was not significantly different than diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ATPγS (D1,obs = 0.026 μm2/s ± 0.002).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical comparison of diffusion coefficients shown in Figure 3C, D.

claim: SWR1 diffusion in the absence of ATP (D1,obs = 0.013 μm2/s ± 0.002) was not different than SWR1 diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ADP (D1,obs = 0.011 μm2/s ± 0.002).
source: Similarly, SWR1 diffusion in the absence of ATP (D1,obs = 0.013 μm2/s ± 0.002) was not different than SWR1 diffusion in the presence of 1 mM ADP (D1,obs = 0.011 μm2/s ± 0.002).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical comparison of diffusion coefficients shown in Figure 3C, D.

claim: ATP decreased the fraction of slow or immobile Cy3-SWR1 molecules.
source: Additionally, we found that ATP decreased the fraction of slow or immobile Cy3-SWR1 molecules, defined as those molecules that show D1 values that are indistinguishable from dCas9 values (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: While 9% of Cy3-SWR1 were slow or immobile in the presence of ATP, 32% were slow or immobile in buffer alone.
source: While 9% of Cy3-SWR1 were slow or immobile in the presence of ATP, 32% were slow or immobile in buffer alone.
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: While SWR1 does not actively translocate on DNA, binding of ATP increases the mobility of SWR1 on DNA.
source: These results show that while SWR1 does not actively translocate on DNA, binding of ATP increases the mobility of SWR1 on DNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data in Figure 3 showing increased diffusion with ATP but no directional movement.

claim: SWR1 binding to DNA is mediated in part by the Swc2 subunit, which harbors a positively charged and unstructured DNA-binding domain (DBD).
source: SWR1 binding to DNA is mediated in part by the Swc2 subunit, which harbors a positively charged and unstructured DNA-binding domain (DBD) (Ranjan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study characterizing Swc2's DNA-binding domain.

claim: Swc2 also diffuses on DNA.
source: We found that Swc2 also diffuses on DNA, however the median diffusion coefficient, D1,obs = 1.04 μm2/s ± 0.09, was approximately 40-fold larger than that of SWR1 in the presence of 1 mM ATP (Figure 4, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-particle tracking experiments on Swc2 DBD shown in Figure 4.

claim: The median diffusion coefficient for Swc2 DBD is D1,obs = 1.04 μm2/s ± 0.09, which was approximately 40-fold larger than that of SWR1 in the presence of 1 mM ATP.
source: We found that Swc2 also diffuses on DNA, however the median diffusion coefficient, D1,obs = 1.04 μm2/s ± 0.09, was approximately 40-fold larger than that of SWR1 in the presence of 1 mM ATP (Figure 4, Materials and methods).
evidence: This value is directly measured from experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The scaling relationship between size and diffusion coefficient is consistent with SWR1 and Swc2 DBD utilizing rotationally coupled sliding.
source: Based on theoretical models of rotation-coupled versus -uncoupled diffusion, the scaling relationship between size and diffusion coefficient is consistent with SWR1 and Swc2 DBD utilizing rotationally coupled sliding (Blainey et al., 2009; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing experimental data to theoretical models, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both SWR1 and Swc2 DBD show increased diffusion with increasing concentrations of potassium chloride.
source: Next, we found that both SWR1 and Swc2 DBD show increased diffusion with increasing concentrations of potassium chloride (Figure 4A), and each showed decreasing binding lifetimes with increasing salt (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4A, B.

claim: Both SWR1 and Swc2 DBD showed decreasing binding lifetimes with increasing salt.
source: Next, we found that both SWR1 and Swc2 DBD show increased diffusion with increasing concentrations of potassium chloride (Figure 4A), and each showed decreasing binding lifetimes with increasing salt (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: Both increased diffusion and decreased binding lifetimes are features of 1D hopping.
source: Both increased diffusion and decreased binding lifetimes are features of 1D hopping, as the more time a protein spends in microscopic dissociation and reassociation the faster it can move on DNA, but also falls off DNA more frequently (Bonnet et al., 2008; Mirny et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical and experimental work on 1D hopping mechanisms.

claim: Competitor DNA can decrease binding lifetime of SWR1.
source: The TIRF assay also shows that competitor DNA can decrease binding lifetime as would be expected for a protein that hops on DNA and may be prone to alternative binding onto competitor DNA (Brown et al., 2016; Gorman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F and supported by citations.

claim: Swc2 DBD experienced shortened dwell-times in the presence of competitor DNA.
source: Like SWR1, Swc2 DBD experienced shortened dwell-times in the presence of competitor DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: In all conditions measured, the median diffusion of SWR1 is below the upper limit with rotation.
source: In all conditions measured, the median diffusion of SWR1 is below the upper limit with rotation (Figure 4C), consistent with much of the observed diffusion coming from SWR1 engaging in rotationally coupled diffusion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing measured diffusion coefficients to theoretical limits in Figure 4C.

claim: Some individual traces have diffusion coefficients that surpass the theoretical maximum with rotation, indicating that there may be alternative modes for engaging with DNA.
source: Nonetheless, some individual traces have diffusion coefficients that surpass this theoretical maximum, indicating that there may be alternative modes for engaging with DNA (e.g., infrequent hopping), which allows it to surpass the upper limit with rotation (Ahmadi et al., 2018; Gorman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 4C and interpreted with reference to prior literature.

claim: Swc2 DBD exhibited median diffusion coefficients below the theoretical maximum with rotation, with some traces having diffusion coefficients above this limit.
source: A similar phenomenon was observed for Swc2 DBD, which also exhibited median diffusion coefficients below the theoretical maximum with rotation, with some traces having diffusion coefficients above this limit (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing measured diffusion coefficients to theoretical limits in Figure 4C.

claim: SWR1 utilizes a majority 1D helically coupled sliding with occasional hopping to diffuse on DNA.
source: These trends are consistent with a model in which SWR1 utilizes a majority 1D helically coupled sliding with occasional hopping (or monkey bar-like movements) to diffuse on DNA (Figure 4D).
evidence: This model is inferred from the combined experimental data on salt dependence, theoretical limits, and barrier bypass experiments.

claim: Out of 106 traces with colocalization events, 67% showed SWR1 moving away from dCas9 toward where it came from as if it was reflected from a boundary.
source: Out of 106 traces with colocalization events, 67% showed SWR1 moving away from dCas9 toward where it came from as if it was reflected from a boundary (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This is quantified from the dual-color tracking experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: 30% of traces showed SWR1 immobile and colocalized with dCas9 for the duration of the trace.
source: Another 30% of traces showed SWR1 immobile and colocalized with dCas9 for the duration of the trace, which we describe as stuck (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is quantified from the dual-color tracking experiments shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Only 3% of all colocalization events exhibited a crossover event.
source: Only 3% of all colocalization events exhibited a crossover event (Figure 5C, E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantified from the dual-color tracking experiments shown in Figure 5C, E.

claim: The ability of dCas9 to block SWR1 diffusion in most encounters further supports a model in which SWR1 mainly engages in helically coupled sliding.
source: The ability of dCas9 to block SWR1 diffusion in most encounters further supports a model in which SWR1 mainly engages in helically coupled sliding (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that SWR1 is blocked by dCas9 in 97% of encounters.

claim: On average, 40 ± 5 nucleosomes were incorporated onto the lambda nucleosome arrays.
source: On average, 40 ± 5 nucleosomes were incorporated onto the lambda nucleosome arrays as shown by nucleosome unwrapping force–distance curves (Figure 6B–E)
evidence: This is measured from force-distance curves shown in Figure 6B-E.

claim: Nucleosomes showed detectable unwrapping at forces 15 pN or greater.
source: nucleosomes showed detectable unwrapping at forces 15 pN or greater (Figure 6B; Brower-Toland et al., 2002; Fierz and Poirier, 2019)
evidence: This is demonstrated by force-distance curves in Figure 6B and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nucleosome unwrapping results in a characteristic lengthening of ~25 nm with each unwrapping event.
source: with a characteristic lengthening of the array by ~25 nm with each unwrapping event (Figure 6C; Spakman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the unwrapping events shown in Figure 6C and supported by a citation.

claim: The mean MSD for SWR1 on naked DNA increases linearly at short time scales (<2 s).
source: The mean MSD for SWR1 on naked DNA increases linearly at short time scales (<2 s), whereas the mean MSD for SWR1 on the lambda nucleosome array plateaus over this same time scale, indicative of confined 1D diffusion (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MSD analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The mean MSD for SWR1 on the lambda nucleosome array plateaus over short time scales (<2 s), indicative of confined 1D diffusion.
source: The mean MSD for SWR1 on naked DNA increases linearly at short time scales (<2 s), whereas the mean MSD for SWR1 on the lambda nucleosome array plateaus over this same time scale, indicative of confined 1D diffusion (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MSD analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: SWR1 on naked DNA has an α = 0.88 over a 2-s time scale.
source: Whereas SWR1 on naked DNA has an α = 0.88 over a 2-s time scale, SWR1 on the lambda array has an α = 0.24 reflecting considerable confinement.
evidence: This is calculated from fitting MSD data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: SWR1 on the lambda array has an α = 0.24 reflecting considerable confinement.
source: Whereas SWR1 on naked DNA has an α = 0.88 over a 2-s time scale, SWR1 on the lambda array has an α = 0.24 reflecting considerable confinement.
evidence: This is calculated from fitting MSD data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The mean MSD for SWR1 on nucleosome arrays appears to approach a limit of 0.054 μm2.
source: By fitting the MSD curve to an exponential function, the mean MSD appears to approach a limit of 0.054 μm2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is calculated from fitting MSD data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The length of DNA to which SWR1 diffusion is confined is approximately 0.23 μm.
source: whereas the length of DNA to which SWR1 diffusion is confined is approximately 0.23 μm, determined from the square root of the MSD limit described above.
evidence: This is calculated from the MSD limit determined from experimental data.

claim: SWR1 diffusion is confined to the space between nucleosomes.
source: These data, therefore, suggest that SWR1 diffusion is confined to the space between nucleosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the confined diffusion behavior observed on nucleosome arrays in Figure 6.

claim: SWR1 slides on DNA, which is a novel finding for a chromatin remodeler.
source: Our single-molecule tracking data show that SWR1 slides on DNA, which is a novel finding for a chromatin remodeler.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, demonstrated by the single-particle tracking experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: SWR1 scans DNA with a diffusion coefficient comparable to other well-characterized proteins that utilize facilitated diffusion.
source: Moreover, SWR1 scans DNA with a diffusion coefficient comparable to other well-characterized proteins that utilize facilitated diffusion to bind specific DNA sequences or lesions (Ahmadi et al., 2018; Blainey et al., 2006; Gorman et al., 2010; Kamagata et al., 2020; Porecha and Stivers, 2008; Tafvizi et al., 2011; Tafvizi et al., 2008; Vestergaard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by comparing the measured diffusion coefficient to values reported in prior literature.

claim: In the yeast genome, there are approximately 61,568 annotated nucleosomes.
source: In the yeast genome, there are approximately 61,568 annotated nucleosomes (Jiang and Pugh, 2009; Kubik et al., 2015), of which 4576 are identified as potential +1 nucleosomes enriched in H2A.Z (Tramantano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior genomic studies.

claim: 4576 nucleosomes are identified as potential +1 nucleosomes enriched in H2A.Z.
source: In the yeast genome, there are approximately 61,568 annotated nucleosomes (Jiang and Pugh, 2009; Kubik et al., 2015), of which 4576 are identified as potential +1 nucleosomes enriched in H2A.Z (Tramantano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior genomic study.

claim: Only 7% of nucleosomes are targets of SWR1 histone exchange.
source: Since only 7% of nucleosomes are targets of SWR1 histone exchange, we believe that +1 nucleosomes use their adjacent NDRs as antennas, promoting SWR1 binding and 1D search to encounter flanking nucleosomes (Mirny et al., 2009).
evidence: This is calculated from the numbers provided (4576/61568) and used to support the hypothesis about NDRs as antennas.

claim: 1D diffusion at NDRs may be an important aspect of SWR1 target search and potentially a common feature for chromatin remodelers that act upon nucleosomes adjacent to the NDR.
source: 1D diffusion at NDRs may be an important aspect of SWR1 target search and potentially a common feature for chromatin remodelers that acts upon nucleosomes adjacent to the NDR.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the study and knowledge of other chromatin remodelers.

claim: Acetylation of the +1 nucleosome may help establish the directionality of the interaction when assessing the two NDR-flanking nucleosomes.
source: While there is evidence that acetylation of the +1 nucleosome may help establish the directionality of the interaction when assessing the two NDR-flanking nucleosomes (Ranjan et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2005), data from our study indicate that even nucleosomes lacking acetylation can reduce the diffusion of the SWR1 complex possibly through nucleosome engagement.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on acetylation effects.

claim: Even nucleosomes lacking acetylation can reduce the diffusion of the SWR1 complex possibly through nucleosome engagement.
source: While there is evidence that acetylation of the +1 nucleosome may help establish the directionality of the interaction when assessing the two NDR-flanking nucleosomes (Ranjan et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2005), data from our study indicate that even nucleosomes lacking acetylation can reduce the diffusion of the SWR1 complex possibly through nucleosome engagement.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on nucleosome arrays shown in Figure 6.

claim: H2A.Z is preferentially enriched at inactive promoters.
source: Additionally, H2A.Z is preferentially enriched at inactive promoters (Li et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Promoter NDR regions from yeast are highly rigid and this unique property helps instruct the chromatin remodeler, INO80, to position nucleosomes at the boundary of the rigid NDR.
source: A sequencing study discovering the intrinsic flexibility of different DNA sequences helped establish that promoter NDR regions from yeast are highly rigid and this unique property compared to gene-body DNA helps instruct the chromatin remodeler, INO80, a close relative of SWR1, to position nucleosomes at the boundary of the rigid NDR helping to establish the defined positioning of the +1 nucleosome (Basu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study on DNA flexibility and INO80.

claim: SWR1 requires ATP to perform the histone exchange reaction.
source: SWR1 requires ATP to perform the histone exchange reaction, and basal levels of ATP hydrolysis when any one of the required substrates for the histone exchange reaction is missing is low (Luk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior biochemical study.

claim: Basal levels of ATP hydrolysis when any one of the required substrates for the histone exchange reaction is missing is low.
source: SWR1 requires ATP to perform the histone exchange reaction, and basal levels of ATP hydrolysis when any one of the required substrates for the histone exchange reaction is missing is low (Luk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior biochemical study.

claim: Binding of nucleotide cofactor has been shown to produce conformational changes in ATPases that can affect their diffusion on DNA.
source: Binding of nucleotide cofactor has been shown to produce conformational changes in ATPases that can affect their diffusion on DNA (Gorman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study on ATPase conformational changes.

claim: The core ATPase domain of SWR1, Swr1, belongs to the SF2 of translocases which have two lobes that switch between an open and closed conformation with ATP binding and hydrolysis.
source: The core ATPase domain of SWR1, Swr1, like other chromatin remodelers, belongs to the SF2 of translocases which have two lobes that switch between an open and closed conformation with ATP binding and hydrolysis (Beyer et al., 2013; Nodelman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Proteins that hop on DNA have increased diffusion with increased monovalent cation concentration.
source: Proteins that hop on DNA therefore have increased diffusion with increased monovalent cation concentration, as a higher screening potential results in more frequent hops.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about hopping mechanisms.

claim: In order for a protein to slide or hop on DNA, the energy barrier (ΔG‡) to break the static interaction and dynamically engage with the DNA must be less than ≈2 kBT.
source: In order for a protein to slide or hop on DNA, the energy barrier (ΔG‡) to break the static interaction and dynamically engage with the DNA following the parameters of either the sliding or hopping model must be less than ≈2 kBT (Ahmadi et al., 2018; Gorman et al., 2007; Slutsky and Mirny, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical and experimental studies on DNA diffusion mechanisms.

claim: Other studies have found that proteins that utilize sliding as the predominant form of 1D diffusion cannot bypass proteins or nucleosomes.
source: Other studies have found that proteins that utilize sliding as the predominant form of 1D diffusion cannot bypass proteins or nucleosomes (Brown et al., 2016; Gorman et al., 2010; Hedglin and O'Brien, 2010), whereas a protein that predominantly hops may be able to bypass these obstacles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on protein diffusion and barrier bypass.

claim: A protein that predominantly hops may be able to bypass obstacles.
source: Other studies have found that proteins that utilize sliding as the predominant form of 1D diffusion cannot bypass proteins or nucleosomes (Brown et al., 2016; Gorman et al., 2010; Hedglin and O'Brien, 2010), whereas a protein that predominantly hops may be able to bypass these obstacles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on protein diffusion mechanisms.

claim: The utilization of hopping diffusion has been described as a trade-off between scanning speed and accuracy, with proven implications in target sequence bypass by the transcription factor LacI.
source: The utilization of hopping diffusion has been described as a trade-off between scanning speed and accuracy, with proven implications in target sequence bypass by the transcription factor LacI (Marklund et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study on LacI diffusion.

claim: Approximately 47% of SWR1 molecules are bound to chromatin and the remainder is performing 3D diffusion.
source: Single-particle tracking in vivo has shown that approximately 47% of SWR1 molecules are bound to chromatin and the remainder is performing 3D diffusion (Ranjan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior in vivo single-particle tracking study.

claim: SWR1 would require 46 ms to scan and encounter a flanking nucleosome by 1D diffusion at 0.024 μm2/s from the center of an average NDR of ~150 bp.
source: Once bound (e.g., near the center of an average NDR of ~150 bp) our findings suggest that SWR1 would require 46 ms (see Materials and methods) to scan and encounter a flanking nucleosome by 1D diffusion at 0.024 μm2/s.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured diffusion coefficient and NDR length.

claim: SWR1 bound to chromatin has a bound-state diffusion coefficient that is ~twofold larger than the diffusion of chromatin itself (SWR1 D bound 0.063 ± 0.0003 μm2/s versus histone H2B D bound 0.028 ± 0.0002 μm2/s).
source: SWR1 bound to chromatin has been shown to have a bound-state diffusion coefficient that is ~twofold larger than the diffusion of chromatin itself (SWR1 D bound 0.063 ± 0.0003 μm2/s versus histone H2B D bound 0.028 ± 0.0002 μm2/s) (Ranjan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior in vivo single-particle tracking study.

claim: Other yeast chromatin remodelers that act on nucleosomes adjacent to the NDR (RSC, SWI/SNF, ISW2, and INO80) are similarly more diffusive than histone H2B in their chromatin-bound states.
source: A later study found that other yeast chromatin remodelers that act on nucleosomes adjacent to the NDR (RSC, SWI/SNF, ISW2, and INO80) are similarly more diffusive than histone H2B in their chromatin-bound states, and are, similar to SWR1, dependent on the ability of their ATPase domains to bind or hydrolyze ATP in order to exhibit this enhanced bound diffusion (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior in vivo study on multiple chromatin remodelers.

claim: When complexed with a canonical nucleosome and the H2A.Z–H2B dimer, SWR1 can rapidly perform the ATP hydrolysis-dependent histone exchange reaction on average in 2.4 s.
source: A single-molecule TIRF study on the molecular mechanism of the SWR1 histone exchange reaction recently reported that when complexed with a canonical nucleosome and the H2A.Z–H2B dimer, SWR1 can rapidly perform the ATP hydrolysis-dependent histone exchange reaction on average in 2.4 s (Poyton et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent single-molecule study.

claim: The fluorescently labeled SWR1 complex maintains full histone exchange activity.
source: We demonstrated that the fluorescently labeled SWR1 complex maintains full histone exchange activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the EMSA assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cy3-labeled Swc7 comigrated with the rest of the SWR1 subunits, demonstrating incorporation of Swc7 back into the SWR1 complex.
source: Subsequent purification on a glycerol gradient revealed that the Cy3-labeled Swc7 comigrated with the rest of the SWR1 subunits, demonstrating incorporation of Swc7 back into the SWR1 complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the glycerol gradient purification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cy3-Swc7 alone exhibited no affinity for 150 bp DNA.
source: Cy3-Swc7 alone exhibited no affinity for 150 bp DNA (data not shown), suggesting that the observed Cy3-signal increase is caused by the full Cy3–SWR1 complex binding to DNA.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, though the data are not shown.

claim: The localization precision is σ = 82 nm.
source: This results in a σ = 82 nm.
evidence: This is calculated from the formula provided in the Materials and methods section using measured parameters.

claim: Lambda DNA tethered at its ends to two optically trapped beads was pulled to a tension of 5 pN, which resulted in a length approximately 92% of its contour length (15.2 µm).
source: Lambda DNA tethered at its ends to two optically trapped beads was pulled to a tension of 5 pN, which resulted in a length approximately 92% of its contour length (15.2 µm).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental condition in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The length per basepair of DNA at 5 pN tension is 0.31 nm.
source: The length per basepair of DNA, 0.31 nm, is therefore slightly shorter than the value at full contour length (Baumann et al., 2000).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental conditions and supported by a citation.

claim: The length of the NDR, 150 bp, in the experimental conditions is approximately 0.047 µm long.
source: The length of the NDR, 150 bp, in our conditions is therefore roughly 0.047 µm long.
evidence: This is calculated from the length per basepair at 5 pN tension.
